opus-5.5.text:
It really comes down to what kind of claim the solution is making. AlphaEvolve works best when there's an automated evaluator, a piece of code that can score a candidate program or construction. For many problems, that evaluator *is* the ground truth. If AlphaEvolve finds a better construction for a combinatorial problem or a more efficient way to multiply matrices, you can check it mathematically. The verification is exact, and you don't need a lab.

The question gets more interesting when the evaluator is a proxy for something in the real world. Take scheduling heuristics for data centers, or optimizing a kernel for hardware. There the scoring function is usually a simulator or a model of the system. A simulator is an approximation, and an optimizer as powerful as AlphaEvolve is very good at finding the gaps between the proxy and reality. So the rule of thumb is that the further your evaluator is from the thing you actually care about, the more you need to close that loop physically. For compute infrastructure, that means deploying carefully, measuring real performance, and making sure the gains hold. For anything touching biology, materials, or chemistry, it means wet-lab or experimental validation, because a simulator's prediction is only a hypothesis.

A few things push us toward real-world validation. One is fidelity: how well we trust the simulator in the regime where the solution lands. Solutions that look strange or sit far from anything we've seen before deserve extra skepticism, because that's often where models break. Another is stakes: if something will run across a fleet or inform a scientific claim, the bar is higher. The third is interpretability. One nice property of AlphaEvolve is that it produces code, so humans can read the solution, understand why it works, and often spot whether it's exploiting a quirk of the evaluator or capturing something real.

So it's a spectrum. Where verification is formal, the evaluator is enough. Where the evaluator is a model of the world, we treat AlphaEvolve's output as a strong candidate, and the physical world gets the final say.

r001.rationale: The response says formal verification can make the evaluator sufficient and that exact mathematical checks need no lab, but it does not clearly state the criterion’s condition that the evaluator perfectly characterizes reality.

r002.rationale: The response says to measure real performance and verify gains hold when the evaluator is a proxy, with the physical world getting the final say.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and the honest answer is that it depends entirely on what the problem is and what the verifier is.

The thing that makes AlphaEvolve work is that we only point it at problems where we can check the answer. It proposes a program, we run it, we score it, and that score is the signal driving the evolutionary search. So the first question I ask is: how faithful is the verifier to reality? For a lot of the problems we've worked on, the verifier is reality. If you're looking for a faster matrix multiplication algorithm, we can check mathematically that the algorithm is correct, and then we can time it. There's no gap between the thing the system optimized and the thing we actually care about. The same is true for the mathematical constructions, the kissing number improvements, the packing problems. The proof of correctness is a computation, and you can go verify it yourself. Those don't need the physical world at all.

Where it gets more interesting is when the verifier is a model of the world rather than the world itself. Take the data center scheduling work with Borg, or the hardware design pieces. There, you're optimizing against a simulator or a set of traces, and a simulator is always an abstraction. The system is very good at finding the slack in whatever objective you hand it, and sometimes that slack is a real improvement and sometimes it's an artifact of the simulation. So the rule we've converged on is roughly: the further the verifier is from the real deployment environment, the more we insist on staged validation. You run it on a small slice of real traffic, you compare against the baseline, you look for the ways the solution could be exploiting something the simulator got wrong.

The other thing I'd say is that we try to design the problem so that the solutions are interpretable. Because AlphaEvolve produces code, not just a black-box policy, engineers can actually read the heuristic it found. That's a form of validation in itself. If a domain expert looks at the solution and says, "I understand why this works," that gives you a lot more confidence than a number on a benchmark. And when they look at it and say, "I have no idea why this is better," that's exactly the signal that you need to go test it in the real system before you trust it.

r001.rationale: The response says that when the verifier matches reality, there is no gap between the optimized score and the real objective, so those solutions do not need physical-world validation.

r002.rationale: It describes testing solutions on real traffic and checking for improvements or artifacts caused by simulator errors, using real-world results to validate the evaluator’s assessment.

astra-6.text:
It depends on what kind of claim the solution is making. If it’s a mathematical or computational claim, and we can verify it with a proof or a reliable program, then we may not need a physical experiment. We can check whether the solution satisfies the constraints and whether it improves the objective we care about.

But if the claim is about the physical world—say, whether a proposed material has a particular property—then doing well in a simulation is not enough. The simulation makes assumptions, and those assumptions may miss something important. You need an experiment to establish that the improvement carries over to reality.

So the key question is: does our evaluator actually establish the claim, or is it only a proxy for what we ultimately want? AlphaEvolve can search for solutions that score well, but that distinction determines what further validation they need.

r001.rationale: The response says a proof or reliable program may suffice for mathematical or computational claims. It does not say physical validation is unnecessary when an evaluator perfectly characterizes reality; for physical-world claims, it says an experiment is needed.

r002.rationale: The response says experiments establish whether a simulated improvement carries over to reality and asks whether the evaluator establishes the claim or is only a proxy, identifying validation as a check on the evaluator’s assessment.

sol-6.1.text:
It depends on what kind of claim the solution is making. If AlphaEvolve proposes a mathematical construction, and we can verify that it satisfies all the required conditions, then we may have everything we need. There isn’t necessarily a physical experiment to do.

But if the claim is about how something will behave in the real world, then the evaluation we give the system is only a proxy. A solution can perform very well in a simulation and still fail because the simulation leaves something out. In that case, you need to test it in the physical world.

So the key question is: does our evaluator establish the thing we actually care about, or does it establish something that we hope predicts it? The gap between those two determines what further validation is needed.

r001.rationale: The response says a verified mathematical construction may need no physical experiment, but it does not state that validation is unnecessary when the computational evaluator is completely trusted to characterize reality perfectly.

r002.rationale: It explains that a simulation is only a proxy and can miss real-world factors, so physical testing checks whether the evaluator’s assessment predicts actual behavior.
